enclosed room.context: Enter was via a single door on one wall, leaving other walls closed off from their surroundings. We might perceive such an enclosed room as a discrete entity, a place where awareness of the external spaces and events occurring beyond its walls is not necessarily present.

cast.definition: The informational content of hardness; a statement or claim about the future state of the world that is made hard by a system.
cast.context: First, what is the hardness about? What is the informational content of the hardness? I will call this the cast. The cast is the 'thing that is hard,' and it always takes the form of a statement or claim about the future.

atom hardness.definition: Hardness sourced from the physical properties of the universe, including matter, physical laws, and natural constants that make certain future states predictable.
atom hardness.context: Atom hardness refers to hardness that is sourced from the physical properties of our universe. This hardness includes not just literal atoms (i.e., matter, physical stuff), but all other properties of nature like physical laws and constants.

institution hardness.definition: Hardness created through organized human behavior, where groups of people act in predictable ways over time to enforce rules and make future states reliable.
institution hardness.context: In other cases, the source of hardness might be an institution. A contract is only hard if there is an institution that makes it so. Groups of people—lawyers, judges, police officers—who share a common understanding of how to work together.

blockchain hardness.definition: A natively digital source of hardness created through cryptography, networked software, and commoditized human incentives that make digital records and programs permanently reliable.
blockchain hardness.context: Recently, we've invented a new way to create hardness: blockchains. Using an elegant combination of cryptography, networked software, and commoditized human incentives, we are able to create software and digital records that have a degree of permanence.

institution.definition: A broad category of organized human groups including legal systems, governments, corporations, and religious bodies that act predictably to create hardness and enforce rules.
institution.context: Institution here is an extremely broad category, including: legal systems, legislatures, police forces, governments, central banks and other monetary authorities, private banks, corporations, startups, religious institutions.

credible neutrality.definition: The property of blockchains where rules are transparent and verifiable, making them appear impartial rather than subject to arbitrary human discretion.
credible neutrality.context: Blockchains can be credibly neutral because their rules are transparent and verifiable, and casts about those rules are made hard by the blockchain itself.

composability.definition: The ability of applications built on blockchains like Ethereum to reliably build on top of each other because their foundations are made hard and will not change.
composability.context: Ethereum enables composability between applications because applications built on Ethereum can be very hard, with high assurances that they will not change. Applications that are deployed on mainnet will stay there, letting developers build on top of what has already been built.

hyperstructures.definition: Protocols built on blockchain hardness that can theoretically run forever without requiring maintenance or central coordination because their foundations are permanently reliable.
hyperstructures.context: Ethereum enables hyperstructures—protocols that can run forever—because blockchains provide a native source of hardness that makes the structures built on top of them extremely likely to persist into the future.

trustless.definition: A property of blockchains where hardness is created without depending on the behavior or discretion of individual people or institutions.
trustless.context: Blockchains can be trustless in the sense that they create hardness without any reliance on the behavior of individual people or institutions.

decentralized finance (defi).definition: Financial systems built on blockchain hardness that recreate complex financial relationships without requiring institutional intermediaries.
decentralized finance (defi).context: Ethereum enables decentralized finance (defi) because it lets us create programmable hardness sufficient to recreate the complex intersecting web of relationships that characterize traditional finance.

web3.definition: An ecosystem of digital services, protocols, and applications whose infrastructure is grounded primarily in blockchain hardness rather than institutional hardness.
web3.context: Ethereum enables web3: an ecosystem of web services, protocols, applications, and communities whose foundations are built primarily on blockchain hardness rather than institutional hardness.

source of hardness.definition: The underlying mechanism or system that makes a cast (future claim) hard; atoms, institutions, or blockchains.
source of hardness.context: Second, there is the source of hardness. The source of hardness is the reason that the cast can be hard in the first place. It is what the cast is made out of: atoms, institutions, or blockchains.

programmable hardness.definition: The ability to customize and create arbitrary future claims that are made reliable through software running on blockchains.
programmable hardness.context: Just as institutions let us create hard casts with any arbitrary content that can be interpreted and executed by humans, Ethereum lets us create hard casts with arbitrary content that can be interpreted and executed by a computer.

cryptographic hardness.definition: Hardness derived from the mathematical properties of cryptographic systems that make it computationally infeasible to forge or alter digital information.
cryptographic hardness.context: The specific cryptographic tools used by blockchains are public and available for study, and generally their properties are very well understood. The cost of attacking the system to subvert it (e.g., through a so-called 51% attack) is known and we can estimate it accurately.

51% attack.definition: An attack on a blockchain where a malicious actor controls over half the network's computing power, allowing them to subvert the system's hardness.
51% attack.context: The cost of attacking the system to subvert it (e.g., through a so-called 51% attack) is known and we can estimate it accurately.

natively digital.definition: Systems or properties that are inherently designed for and dependent on digital technology and internet infrastructure.
natively digital.context: Blockchains are natively digital. They create hardness about software, data, and programs. Anyone with an internet connection can access and interact with a blockchain.

mainnet.definition: The main operational blockchain network where applications are deployed with high assurance of permanence.
mainnet.context: Applications that are deployed on mainnet will stay there, letting developers build on top of what has already been built, with high confidence that those foundations can never crumble beneath them.

atoms, institutions, and blockchains (ai.definition: The three sources of hardness available to human civilization for creating predictability and reliability in complex systems.
atoms, institutions, and blockchains (ai.context: Atoms, Institutions, and Blockchains are some of the raw materials this infrastructure is built with. Just as an architect must carefully plan not only the design of a building, but also the materials used to construct that design, so must we carefully consider the materials for our civilization's infrastructure.

unprotocolized knowledge.definition: Information and theories that develop and circulate outside formal institutional knowledge production systems, often through internet communities, influencers, and amateur researchers rather than peer review or academic validation.
unprotocolized knowledge.context: There's something powerful about how online seed oil researchers have developed their hypotheses in an unprotocolized way. Seed oils are at the center of a variety of theories, identified as the culprit behind issues ranging from the obesity epidemic to chronic disease.

knowledge protocols.definition: Formal systems and procedures through which societies organize, validate, and legitimize information, including peer review, credentials, teaching, and empirical methods.
knowledge protocols.context: It is only because of these shared, recognized protocols—teaching, refereed publication, credentials, and empiricism, to name a few—that our society construes itself as knowing anything at all.

populist paradigms.definition: Popular, contested theories and ideas that gain widespread traction outside academic institutions, often spreading through internet communities and challenging established scientific paradigms.
populist paradigms.context: These 'populist paradigms,' to twist Thomas Kuhn's term, present a dual challenge. On the one hand, they obviously have spread largely outside the university, bypassing and thus failing to meet the rigorous standards for adjudication that typically accompany scientific claims.

paradigm refugees.definition: Scientists and researchers who are systematically excluded from grants and publishing opportunities because their work challenges the dominant paradigm in their field, forcing them to abandon their original research.
paradigm refugees.context: The decades-long silent embargo forced some researchers to pivot to other topics, creating a class of 'paradigm refugees' unable to continue their original work in a hostile environment.

reasonable insufficiency.definition: The quality of protocols that have become over-successful and now generate unintended maladaptive problems that require further protocol evolution and adaptation.
reasonable insufficiency.context: Perhaps this quality of protocols might be called their reasonable insufficiency: The emergence of unmanaged maladaptive phenomena around too-successful protocols.

republic of letters.definition: A historical intellectual network of 15th-century scholars who shared thoughts, news, and responses across national boundaries through written correspondence, laying groundwork for modern scholarly communication.
republic of letters.context: As 15th-century scholars shared thoughts, news, and responses across national boundaries, they began to understand themselves as participating in a global scholarly conversation, the Republic of Letters.

epistemic tribalism.definition: A condition where information and truth-claims are evaluated primarily through allegiance to ideological or social groups rather than through objective evidence or reasoning.
epistemic tribalism.context: To members of the establishment, the internet's superspeed and superabundance of information creates a condition of 'epistemic tribalism' or 'post-truth.'

context collapse.definition: The phenomenon where the internet eliminates distinctions between academic and public spheres, causing information and communication designed for one audience to reach multiple, unintended audiences simultaneously.
context collapse.context: The alternative view is more realistic and more optimistic: the internet merely collapses the context between academia and the public, leading to new information behaviors that our knowledge production protocols aren't designed to handle.

feral scholars.definition: Unaffiliated amateur researchers and fact-checkers who investigate, verify, and circulate information independently, often in response to gaps or distrust in mainstream academic institutions.
feral scholars.context: Combine this with 'feral scholars' who fact-check, research, and circulate supposedly reputable information in response to the drama.

internet of beefs.definition: A social media ecosystem characterized by ongoing, highly publicized conflicts and disputes between public figures and their followers, often organized around ideological or lifestyle positions.
internet of beefs.context: In the chaotic space outside the jurisdiction of scholarly protocols, in the subscriber lists of influencers' Patreons, a horde of enthusiasts comes into play. Here is where the dynamics resemble less a scientific forum and more the 'Internet of Beefs.'

coercive citation.definition: A predatory publishing practice where journal editors pressure authors to cite articles that benefit the journal's impact scores, even when not directly relevant to the work.
coercive citation.context: Journals, too, exhibit this overeffective quality, having extended far beyond their original function... employing 'coercive citation': editors strong-arming authors to cite articles that benefit their journals' impact scores.

pre-paradigm theory.definition: A competing set of hypotheses and explanations that has not yet achieved the status of an established scientific paradigm but may offer viable alternatives to dominant theoretical frameworks.
pre-paradigm theory.context: Nevertheless, these speculations may collectively be compelling enough to be considered a viable pre-paradigm theory.

dyoresearchers.definition: Do-it-yourself researchers who conduct their own experiments, analysis, and investigations independent of institutional affiliation or formal credentials.
dyoresearchers.context: The products of intellectual labor now live freely online, inspiring swaths of DYOResearchers.

citizen science.definition: Scientific research conducted by non-professional scientists, often amateurs or hobbyists, who contribute data collection, analysis, or experimentation under the framework of formal studies.
citizen science.context: Recent improvements in mobile sensors and smartphones have unlocked new opportunities for citizen science and crowdsourcing.

datafication.definition: The process of converting various aspects of human experience and activity into quantifiable data that can be recorded, analyzed, and used in research and decision-making.
datafication.context: The increasing datafication of health via biometrics points to future evolutions that may be possible for both scientific and internet health communities.

biomonitoring devices.definition: Wearable or portable technologies that measure and track biological indicators such as heart rate, sleep patterns, and other health metrics for personal health tracking or research purposes.
biomonitoring devices.context: Widely available biomonitoring devices could bring down the high cost of quantified selfhood.

participatory science.definition: Scientific research conducted with direct involvement and collaboration from non-professional community members in design, data collection, and evaluation of results.
participatory science.context: the internet making possible a 'global spasm of participatory science.'

epistemic uncertainty.definition: A state of doubt or lack of certainty about what can be known, believed, or validated as true within an information environment.
epistemic uncertainty.context: As it stands, we lack the organizing models necessary to deal with the epistemic uncertainty they create to validate their ideas.

quantified selfhood.definition: The practice of tracking, measuring, and analyzing detailed personal data about one's own body, behavior, and health through devices and self-monitoring.
quantified selfhood.context: Widely available biomonitoring devices could bring down the high cost of quantified selfhood.

workplace productivity protocols.definition: Intentional patterns of human behavior designed to increase an organization's capability to outperform itself, prescribing a choreography for objects, bodies, and brains across meetings and communications.
workplace productivity protocols.context: Borrowing from this framing, workplace productivity protocols can be defined as intentional patterns of human behavior that increase the capability of an organization to outperform itself. These protocols prescribe a choreography for objects and bodies and brains and brains, a dance notation spanning months of run time on the stage of meeting rooms and emails.
workplace productivity protocols.source: Exit to Protocol: A Future After Retirement

protocol dysphoria.definition: A state of dissatisfaction or distress experienced by workers when inhabiting ossified or misaligned productivity protocols that no longer serve their actual work needs.
protocol dysphoria.context: A protocolized framing of a bullshit job would be any worker experiencing what Summer of Protocols researcher Angela Walch calls protocol dysphoria.
protocol dysphoria.source: Exit to Protocol: A Future After Retirement

protocol identity.definition: The particular role and set of responsibilities a worker assumes when entering a workplace as part of the larger system of protocols that govern organizational behavior.
protocol identity.context: These organizations are in effect systems of protocols that a worker inhabits when entering a workplace, taking on a particular protocol identity depending on their role.
protocol identity.source: Exit to Protocol: A Future After Retirement

protocol evolution.definition: The continuous improvement and adaptation of protocols through the evolutionary cycle of birth, mutation, selection, and death, similar to how internet protocols develop.
protocol evolution.context: If workplace productivity protocols have similar attributes to internet protocols wherein nobody owns them, everybody can use them, and anybody can improve them, then like internet protocols, they attract continuous improvement through the same evolutionary cycle of birth, mutation, selection, and death.
protocol evolution.source: Exit to Protocol: A Future After Retirement

exit to protocol.definition: A form of organizational retirement in which an organization ceases operations while publicly sharing its workplace protocols and operational knowledge, allowing new communities and organizations to inherit and evolve these patterns.
exit to protocol.context: Instead, through retiring and sharing some of its workplace protocols publically, this exit may shape many and new communities. This we might call an exit to protocol.
exit to protocol.source: Exit to Protocol: A Future After Retirement

whale fall.definition: An ecological process where a dead whale sinks to the ocean floor and its decomposition creates a nutrient-rich habitat that enables the rapid evolution of new species adapted to those conditions.
whale fall.context: An exit to protocol could be compared to a whale fall in ocean ecosystems, where the death of a whale and its subsequent decay process after falling to the ocean floor creates an energy-rich habitat and frees up nutrients to incubate rapidly evolving new life forms.
whale fall.source: Exit to Protocol: A Future After Retirement

adaptive radiation.definition: The ecological process by which new species rapidly evolve and diversify in response to the novel environmental conditions created by a whale fall or similar nutrient-rich habitat.
adaptive radiation.context: New species are commonly created through this process, known as adaptive radiation.
adaptive radiation.source: Exit to Protocol: A Future After Retirement

exit to community.definition: A movement that helps startups mature into community ownership by their stakeholders rather than pursuing acquisition or public stock offerings.
exit to community.context: Misaligned-incentive bullshit jobs might find a solution in the movement of Exit to Community, a movement that helps startups 'aim to mature into ownership by their community of stakeholders' rather than 'aiming for an acquisition by a more established company or a public stock offering.'
exit to community.source: Exit to Protocol: A Future After Retirement

role in a box.definition: A protocol system design that conveys the people and their relationships to data, spaces, and other people by encapsulating a role with preset levels of access, permissions, and incentives within an organization.
role in a box.context: The protocol system conveys the people and their relationship to data, spaces, and other people, describing it as a 'role in a box' with different preset levels of access, permissions, and incentives to represent and augment the organization.
role in a box.source: Exit to Protocol: A Future After Retirement

hats protocol.definition: A digital protocol that empowers groups to delegate responsibilities to contributors while giving them necessary authorities and installing accountability mechanisms to ensure task completion in distributed work environments.
hats protocol.context: Hats empowers groups to get things done by delegating responsibilities to the right contributors, giving them the hard and soft authorities they need to do their work, and installing real-time accountability mechanisms to ensure people follow through.
hats protocol.source: Exit to Protocol: A Future After Retirement

bullshit jobs.definition: Forms of employment that are so completely pointless, unnecessary, or pernicious that even employees cannot justify their existence, though they feel obliged to pretend otherwise.
bullshit jobs.context: Rather than experiencing protocol death through abandonment, the agile industrial complex creates an entire workforce engaged in what David Graeber called bullshit jobs—a group of workers kept employed under imbalanced power structures that encourage keeping up the pretenses of unnecessary work.
bullshit jobs.source: Exit to Protocol: A Future After Retirement

intellectual monopoly capitalism.definition: An economic system where corporations prioritize the capture and management of intellectual assets and knowledge as their most strategic resources, with learning itself becoming the primary corporate goal.
intellectual monopoly capitalism.context: The rise of intellectual monopoly capitalism presents a new buyer of workplace protocols for the sake of the protocols themselves, and not necessarily for their resulting productivity.
intellectual monopoly capitalism.source: Exit to Protocol: A Future After Retirement

bannister effect.definition: A phenomenon where organizational or emergent groups feel more confident about adopting new methods after seeing that success was possible with them, inspired by a celebratory rather than crisis-driven retirement.
bannister effect.context: Retirement that ends on a celebratory note allows for the Bannister Effect, where organizations or emergent groups may feel more confident about adopting the new methods through seeing that it was possible to achieve success with them.
bannister effect.source: Exit to Protocol: A Future After Retirement

metawork.definition: The documentation and operational processes of how work is performed, distinct from the actual work product itself; the practices and systems that enable and organize the primary work.
metawork.context: Such generous documentation and sharing of the metawork of a studio or any place of knowledge work is beyond rare in an industry where most documents are labeled confidential and nondisclosure agreements are signed.
metawork.source: Exit to Protocol: A Future After Retirement

selection pressures.definition: Institutional, structural, or incentive-based forces that constrain how protocols can evolve and adapt, often preventing necessary mutations that would improve protocol fitness.
selection pressures.context: However, the power dynamics in a workplace can impose selection pressures that prevent protocols from adapting through mutation, resulting in productivity protocols that become unfit for purpose.
selection pressures.source: Exit to Protocol: A Future After Retirement

protocol death.definition: The discontinuation or abandonment of a protocol when it is no longer needed because environmental conditions have changed or the behavior it codified is no longer necessary.
protocol death.context: In the same way that a safety protocol is no longer needed because a hazard has been removed, a workplace productivity protocol is not needed when human behaviors no longer account for resulting productivity.
protocol death.source: Exit to Protocol: A Future After Retirement

dumb storage.definition: A practice of archiving organizational knowledge and resources in sealed or inaccessible formats that prevent their use or evolution by others, keeping them dormant for potential future recreation.
dumb storage.context: An organization might have kept confidential to maximize future consulting fees, or as Friend puts it in Good Death, sealed in 'dumb storage' so that the 'fantasy of recreating the thing being archived potentially exists.'
dumb storage.source: Exit to Protocol: A Future After Retirement

agile industrial complex.definition: A self-perpetuating ecosystem of consultants, thought leaders, and institutions that profit from continuous promotion and implementation of agile methodologies, creating perverse incentives that prevent protocol evolution.
agile industrial complex.context: This stuckness has characteristics comparable to the ossification of internet protocols. Agile development expert Daniel Mezick's 2016 essay, The Agile Industrial Complex, presents a fantastic case study of how a productivity protocol system has stagnated.
agile industrial complex.source: Exit to Protocol: A Future After Retirement

misaligned incentives.definition: Organizational structures or reward systems where individual workers' incentives diverge from the overall organization's actual productivity needs, contributing to the creation of unnecessary work.
misaligned incentives.context: Flunkies, duct tapers, and type 2 taskmasters exist as a result of misaligned incentives and unbalanced power structures.
misaligned incentives.source: Exit to Protocol: A Future After Retirement

safety protocols.definition: Intentional patterns of constraint on human behavior designed to reduce injury, disease, and death in work environments.
safety protocols.context: I define these as intentional patterns of constraint on human behavior that reduce injury, disease, and death. Safety protocols have evolved in lockstep with changes in the industrial environment.

dynamic non-event.definition: A sustained absence of accidents or negative outcomes resulting from successful human actions and moment-to-moment adjustments, which our brains fail to notice because they lack the discrete, eventful quality of accidents.
dynamic non-event.context: Safety is a dynamic non-event. Talking about safety (and health) is difficult because it is a sustained absence of events, not an event itself.

limit of unacceptable performance.definition: A threshold below which action outcomes become noticeable to human attention and trigger awareness or concern, distinguishing successful from failed performances.
limit of unacceptable performance.context: After a while, the only actions that catch our attention are those with outcome values below the 'limit of unacceptable performance'.

protocol-based social order.definition: A social arrangement with new norms, divisions of labor, and decision-making hierarchies that emerge to enforce and sustain behavioral constraints established by protocols.
protocol-based social order.context: New norms, divisions of labor, and decision-making hierarchies emerge to enforce such constraints. This results in a new protocol-based social order.

chokedamp.definition: Carbonic acid gas (CO2) found in coal mines that acts as an asphyxiant, historically identified as a hazard when a candle flame dimmed or extinguished near floor level.
chokedamp.context: chokedamp: stythe, damp, or blackdamp; carbonic acid gas; an asphyxiant gas. Chokedamp is heavier than air; miners would hold a candle near the floor. If it dimmed or went out, it was time to go.

firedamp.definition: Methane gas (carburetted hydrogen) found in coal mines that is highly explosive, historically addressed by miners preemptively igniting gas buildups.
firedamp.context: firedamp: methane gas/carburetted hydrogen; a highly explosive gas. Miners avoided firedamp by preemptively igniting buildups.

afterdamp.definition: A mixture of carbon monoxide, firedamp, and nitrogen produced after mine explosions that acts as both an asphyxiant and poisonous gas.
afterdamp.context: afterdamp: mix of carbon monoxide, firedamp, and nitrogen; an asphyxiant and poisonous gas.

stinkdamp.definition: Hydrogen sulfide gas found in coal mines, a poisonous gas historically identified by its distinctive odor.
stinkdamp.context: stinkdamp: hydrogen sulfide; a poisonous gas.

bell pit.definition: An early method of coal extraction from the 13th century using a narrow vertical shaft with a widened bottom chamber, abandoned once structural instability appeared and a new shaft was sunk nearby.
bell pit.context: As early as the 13th century, Europeans started to mine coal in bell pits. Miners sunk bell pits to about 30 feet below ground, with a narrow mouth, and dug wider at the bottom.

drift mine.definition: An early coal mining method in which miners dug a near-horizontal slope into a hillside or cliff rather than sinking a vertical shaft, used in terrain where vertical shafts were impractical.
drift mine.context: Drift mines were another early method of coal extraction. Miners dug a near-horizontal slope into a hillside or cliff, rather than digging a vertical shaft in a field.

piece wage.definition: A compensation system in which workers are paid based on the amount of work output (e.g., coal produced) rather than time spent working, creating economic incentives to prioritize productivity over safety.
piece wage.context: miners were often paid a piece wage (by the amount of coal produced, rather than time spent mining). Lack of supervision plus the incentive of piece wages led miners to trade safety for productivity.

the carbon flywheel.definition: The period (1700-1850 A.D.) when the introduction of steam engines and industrial machinery created a self-reinforcing cycle of increased coal demand and production expansion.
the carbon flywheel.context: After centuries of incremental progress, the coal industry had a big bang. With the industrial revolution came steam engines, boilers, coal furnaces, new machinery, and cheaper steel. These technologies enabled a new flywheel of productivity in the coal industry.

root cause analysis.definition: An investigative method used after industrial accidents to identify the underlying cause of failures, initially assumed to be human error before researchers shifted focus to systemic and organizational factors.
root cause analysis.context: First, root cause analysis led safety experts to assume incidents were being caused by human error. If the technology is safe, then it must be the humans who mess up.

safety culture.definition: The collective values, attitudes, and practices within an organization that prioritize and reinforce safe behavior, as distinct from technical engineering approaches to safety.
safety culture.context: The focus turned to sociology instead of psychology. Protocols to improve 'safety culture' came about. Take Five (taking a few minutes to consider the risks and safety measures required for a task), Safety Walk (management walking through a workplace to identify and address hazards), Poka-Yoke...

systems theory (in accident prevention).definition: An approach holding that accidents result from unexpected interactions between tightly coupled components within complex systems and are therefore inherently unpredictable and 'normal' despite prevention efforts.
systems theory (in accident prevention).context: Finally, systems theory came along—holding that 'unexpected interactions' between 'tightly coupled' components within a system cause accidents, and that such accidents are unpredictable. Ultimately, experts found that accidents are 'normal.'

normal accidents.definition: The concept that accidents are inherent and inevitable consequences of complex, tightly coupled systems despite rigorous safety measures, as both preventable and unprevantable phenomena coexist.
normal accidents.context: These two statements are both true: all accidents are preventable and we cannot prevent all accidents.

health protocols.definition: Behavioral constraints designed to prevent cumulative, irreparable damage and long-term disease rather than discrete workplace injuries, addressing chronic conditions and lifestyle risk factors.
health protocols.context: Health is, first, about avoiding cumulative, irreparable damage. Having a pet rattlesnake is unsafe. Working a stressful job that drives you to smoke is unhealthy.

tinkering (protocol design).definition: The intentional, incremental modification of existing protocols by adding or adjusting specific steps, characterized by moderate speed and magnitude of change relative to design or error-based mutation.
tinkering (protocol design).context: To tinker is to intentionally mutate a protocol in some way. For example, one could add a step to a workplace inspection checklist. The pace of mutation by tinkering is likely slower than by memetic error. But it is faster and less dramatic than protocol design.

protocol design.definition: The intentional creation or comprehensive redesign of protocols to be substantially different from existing protocols, characterized by the strongest magnitude of mutation but high risk of rejection if too radical.
protocol design.context: Protocol design, which is creating or changing a protocol so that it is unique from existing protocols. The strength of mutations from design easily places protocols into the realm of infeasibility, where actors will reject them.

protocol atrophy.definition: The gradual decline and death of a protocol through disuse when it is no longer actively performed or reinforced by the social network.
protocol atrophy.context: Like muscles, without use, a protocol atrophies; for a protocol to die, it needs only to not be used.

hazard creation (sources).definition: The three primary drivers that generate new workplace dangers: environmental change, technological progress including knowledge, and shifts in the social order and power distribution.
hazard creation (sources).context: New protocols emerge when we encounter newly created hazards. There are three sources of hazard creation. The first source of hazard creation in the model is environmental change... The second source of hazard creation is technological progress... The third source of hazard creation is change in the social order.

latency period.definition: The delayed interval between occupational exposure to a hazard (such as asbestos) and the clinical manifestation of disease, complicating causal attribution and health protocol development.
latency period.context: causality is difficult to prove given the long timespan between exposure and disease (for example, asbestosis has a latency period of 15 to 30 years), and a mechanism of harm is often below the level of human perception.
